units.policy: The university offers Copyleaks AI text and plagiarism detection software within D2L; the guide notes it flags text edited with Grammarly or copied from Google Translate.

units.fit_note: A: Describes the tool and its false-flag caveat; no rule on how it is used. B: Notes that detector flags legitimate tools; does not say detectors must not be relied on.

units.passage: We don't believe that there is a tool available that can definitively detect AI use in student work.
units.why: "We don't believe that there is a tool available that can definitively detect AI use in student work" says detectors are unreliable (P39).

units.passage: We discourage efforts to submit all student work to a system to attempt to determine if AI was used.
units.why: "We discourage efforts to submit all student work to a system to attempt to determine if AI was used" advises against detection screening, P39 (not relying on detectors).

units.passage: AI Detection Tools – Faculty must exercise caution with AI detection tools, as misidentifications can occur.
units.why: "misidentifications can occur" with AI detection tools, so faculty "must exercise caution". Signals detector unreliability, P39 (caution rather than a ban).
units.fit_note: Asks for caution rather than saying detectors will not be used. Calls for caution about detector error rather than saying detectors will not be used.

units.passage: UT does not endorse AI-detection software and holds no central contract for it.
units.why: The FAQ says 'UT does not endorse AI-detection software and holds no central contract for it', so the university gives instructors no sanctioned detector; closest type is P39 (do not rely on detectors), though it states non-endorsement rather than unreliability.
units.fit_note: States non-endorsement and no central contract, not that detectors are unreliable or cannot be used as proof.

units.passage: However, as AI- generated content continues to evolve, these tools are inherently imperfect and prone to false positives and false negatives.
units.why: "inherently imperfect and prone to false positives and false negatives" says detectors are unreliable, so P39.

units.passage: While these reports can be useful for examining the use of unauthorized or inappropriate resources, false positives and negatives do occur.
units.why: "False positives and negatives do occur." The page admits detector error as a reason not to depend on it, which is P39.
units.fit_note: Detectors are described as useful but fallible rather than rejected.

units.passage: Because automated AI detection is unreliable and can produce harmful false positives that undermine trust, it is strongly discouraged as a primary basis for academic integrity determinations.
units.why: AI detection "is unreliable and can produce harmful false positives" and is "strongly discouraged as a primary basis", so P39 (do not rely on detectors); it stops short of banning detectors.
units.fit_note: Strongly discourages detection as a primary basis instead of ruling it out entirely.

units.passage: At this time, we do not recommend faculty rely on detection tools
units.policy: The university does not recommend that faculty rely on detection tools.
units.why: 'we do not recommend faculty rely on detection tools' is a recommendation against relying on detectors, P39.

units.passage: Unreliable results, including false positives (human work flagged as AI) and false negatives (AI-generated work going undetected)
units.policy: Detection tools give unreliable results, including false positives (human work flagged as AI) and false negatives (AI-generated work going undetected).
units.why: The reasons list 'Unreliable results, including false positives ... and false negatives'; a statement that detectors are unreliable, P39.

units.passage: Generative AI detection tools (such as ZeroGPT, etc.) are designated as DO NOT USE by OneIT because a University enterprise tool is not available, nor is one recommended at this time
units.policy: Generative AI detection tools (such as ZeroGPT) are designated DO NOT USE by OneIT because no University enterprise tool is available or recommended.
units.why: The detection section says tools like ZeroGPT are 'designated as DO NOT USE by OneIT' as they are error-prone and fail reliability standards; detectors are unreliable and should not be used, P39.

units.passage: Both free and paid products available on the market are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards
units.policy: Both free and paid generative AI detection products are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards.
units.why: The text says detection products 'are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards' and do not ensure privacy; this is the reasoning behind the ban and a statement of unreliability (P39); the privacy part is the fit note.

units.passage: However, in spring 2023 semester, MBECTE recommended that faculty not rely on Turnitin’s Originality score to detect all AI usage due to reported reliability issues
units.why: MBECTE 'recommended that faculty not rely on Turnitin's Originality score to detect all AI usage due to reported reliability issues', which is a caution against relying on a detector (P39), not a ban.

units.passage: 5. Ditch Detection Tools
units.policy: Instructors should not use AI-detection tools.
units.why: The heading '5. Ditch Detection Tools' tells instructors not to use AI detectors, so P39 (do not rely on detectors) applies.

units.passage: AI-detection tools have repeatedly proven to be unreliable and inaccurate
units.why: 'AI-detection tools have repeatedly proven to be unreliable and inaccurate, often yielding false alarms flagging student work' gives the reason detectors are not relied on: P39.

units.passage: Based on current technological capabilities, traditional plagiarism checkers are not reliable sources of generative AI detection and publicly available AI detection tools may compromise student privacy protections.
units.why: "traditional plagiarism checkers are not reliable sources of generative AI detection" says detectors cannot be relied on; P39.

units.passage: Vanderbilt currently does not offer any institutionally supported AI detection tools, and many third-party detection tools have unknown privacy and data usage policies.
units.why: "Vanderbilt currently does not offer any institutionally supported AI detection tools" states the university does not provide a detector; P39 is closest, though this is a factual statement about provision.
units.fit_note: Reports non-provision of detectors rather than telling instructors not to rely on them. States the university supplies no detector, rather than saying detector output is unreliable as proof.

units.passage: Lack of public-facing, detailed methodologies and standards for detecting AI-generated text.
units.why: "Lack of public-facing, detailed methodologies" in detectors such as Turnitin is a reason detectors are untrustworthy; P39.

units.passage: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT cannot reliably detect unauthorized AI use.
units.why: "Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT cannot reliably detect unauthorized AI use" tells instructors not to use chatbots as detectors; P39.

units.passage: Additionally, strategies such as comparing a student's work to an AI-generated response to the assignment prompt does not yield reliable results due to the variability of AI-generated outputs.
units.why: "comparing a student's work to an AI-generated response to the assignment prompt does not yield reliable results" says a specific detection technique fails; P39.

units.passage: Don’t expect a technological solution to the challenges of AI
units.why: "Don't expect a technological solution ... AI detectors ... are not uniformly reliable" says detectors cannot be relied on, P39.

units.passage: While AI detectors do exist (ChatGPT’s creators have made one), they are not uniformly reliable—and like other AI tools, will only get better over time.
units.why: 'While AI detectors do exist ... they are not uniformly reliable' says not to rely on detectors. P39 fits.

units.passage: certain academic integrity detection tools are known to have biases by incorrectly flagging writing by students for whom English is not their first-learned language
units.why: The sentence says integrity detection tools have "biases by incorrectly flagging writing by students for whom English is not their first-learned language"; it warns that detectors are unreliable, so P39 with the bias angle noted.
units.fit_note: Frames detector unreliability as bias against non-native English writers rather than as a rule not to rely on detectors.

units.passage: The University discourages instructors from using Gen-AI detectors for the purpose of detecting academic fraud.
units.policy: The University discourages instructors from using Gen-AI detectors for the purpose of detecting academic fraud.
units.why: "The University discourages instructors from using Gen-AI detectors for the purpose of detecting academic fraud" states that detectors should not be relied on, P39.

units.passage: these [detecting] tools are notoriously unreliable and hence using them is usually counterproductive and can be risky.
units.policy: Gen-AI detecting tools are notoriously unreliable and hence using them is usually counterproductive and can be risky (task force report, p. 6).
units.why: The task force report is quoted: "these [detecting] tools are notoriously unreliable and hence using them is usually counterproductive and can be risky." Reason for not relying on detectors, P39.

units.passage: Gen-AI detectors have not been shown to be reliable, and the University discourages instructors from using these tools to detect academic fraud.
units.policy: Gen-AI detectors have not been shown to be reliable, and the University discourages instructors from using them to detect academic fraud.
units.why: "Gen-AI detectors have not been shown to be reliable, and the University discourages instructors from using these tools" repeats the detector stance to students. P39.

units.passage: Currently, the accuracy of tools that purportedly detect GenAI use is not guaranteed. There are instances where these tools fail to detect GenAI use, may not accurately distinguish between content that is generated by humans versus generated by AI, and may generate false positive or negative results.
units.why: "the accuracy of tools that purportedly detect GenAI use is not guaranteed" says detectors are unreliable, so P39.

units.passage: These tools may also exhibit inherent biases that can negatively impact certain groups of students (e.g., non-native English writers, etc.), creating issues of fairness.
units.why: "These tools may also exhibit inherent biases that can negatively impact certain groups of students ... creating issues of fairness" adds a fairness reason against detectors, so P39.
units.fit_note: Gives a bias and fairness reason, beyond accuracy.

units.passage: Although these tools may provide some perspective on whether or not student submissions were created with AI, they will never be 100% accurate, and several studies have demonstrated that they can generate both “false positives” and “false negatives” when attempting to detect AI-created content, especially when applied to the work of non-native English speakers.
units.why: Detection tools 'will never be 100% accurate' and give false positives and negatives: unreliable detectors (P39).

units.passage: Reports from AI detection tools may inform your conversations with students regarding inappropriate use of generative AI, but relying solely on detection tools to “catch” someone using AI is likely to lead to ineffective and stressful interactions with students.
units.why: 'relying solely on detection tools to catch someone using AI is likely to lead to ineffective and stressful interactions': do not rely only on detectors (P39).

units.passage: Due to these concerns, Virginia Tech has not licensed or endorsed any specific platforms for detecting generative AI, and TLOS recommends caution when using these tools.
units.why: 'Virginia Tech has not licensed or endorsed any specific platforms for detecting generative AI' and TLOS 'recommends caution' with them (P39).

units.passage: Please also refrain from using AI detection software to check students’ assignments/exams, as the Office for Undergraduate Academic Integrity does not accept AI detection reports as a form of evidence for Honor Code cases.
units.why: 'Please also refrain from using AI detection software to check students' assignments/exams' is a ban for instructors on detectors (P39).
units.fit_note: Detector reports are not accepted as evidence at all, stricter than the 'supporting only' wording on the OUAI syllabus page.

units.passage: Additionally, the unreliability of AI detection tools creates enforcement dilemmas, while the opacity of large language models makes meaningful validation of AI-assisted research extremely difficult, especially in qualitative methodologies where interpretive nuance is essential.
units.why: 'the unreliability of AI detection tools creates enforcement dilemmas' (P39).

units.passage: AI detection tools can produce false positives, complicating enforcement.
units.why: 'AI detection tools can produce false positives, complicating enforcement.' says detectors are unreliable, P39.

units.passage: Remember: While instructors have the right to prohibit the use of AI tools, no technology can reliably identify unauthorized student use of AI
units.why: 'no technology can reliably identify unauthorized student use of AI' says detectors cannot be relied on, P39.

units.passage: Because tools to detect GenAI are often unreliable, some respondents noted that students take advantage of these limitations when they submit assignments, making enforcement especially challenging
units.why: 'tools to detect GenAI are often unreliable' reports detector unreliability (P39); informs.

units.passage: Still, this tool has notable limitations in identifying AI-generated content.
units.why: 'this tool has notable limitations in identifying AI-generated content' and 'false positives' - the report says SafeAssign is unreliable for AI text (P39); informs.

units.passage: Avoid generative AI detection tools; they are imperfect at best, carry the risk of false positives, have been shown to be biased against non-native English speakers, and will not prevent students from using these tools.
units.why: "Avoid generative AI detection tools; they are imperfect at best, carry the risk of false positives, have been shown to be biased against non-native English speakers" tells instructors not to rely on detectors, P39.

units.passage: UW–Madison has decided not to offer an enterprise tool for AI detection due to these issues
units.policy: UW–Madison has decided not to offer an enterprise tool for AI detection due to these issues.
units.why: 'UW–Madison has decided not to offer an enterprise tool for AI detection' states an institutional decision on detectors (P39).
